speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR SUBSIDY ON SURPLUS FLUID MILK
speechtext: The government's program as announced entails a basic distribution of functions as between federal and provincial responsibilities. Inasmuch as the provinces already exercise a responsibility for quotas and price levels of fluid milk the fluid milk producer and his support are clearly and primarily a provincial responsibility. I believe that the distribution of responsibilities, with the provinces assuming the responsibility for support of the fluid milk producer and the federal government assuming responsibility for the support of the manufacturing milk producer, will in the long run serve the best interests of the dairy farmers of Canada.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR SUBSIDY ON SURPLUS FLUID MILK

If any province in its wisdom, as happened in Ontario this past year, feels that it wishes to subsidize fluid milk producers at figures over and above their production quotas, and basic prices, that of course is a decision that must be made by that province's government.

The first part of clause 6 reads as follows:
Officers and men who were members of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army or the Royal Canadian Air Force immediately prior to the coming into force of this Part are, subject to the provisions of the National Defence Act, members of the Canadian Forces.
This is one of the compulsory features which have been introduced into this bill. As
[Mr. Hellyer.J
DEBATES	April 24, 1967
soon as it becomes law the members of the navy, army and air force will be shifted into forces to be known as the Canadian Forces. We discussed this during defence committee hearings, and I think it would be worth while to re-emphasize the subject of those discussions at this time, because there are many more members present to give it their attention.
During the committee hearings 1 moved two amendments to this clause, which were voted down in the normal fashion by Liberal members voting against any of our proposals. I intend to put those proposals before the committee of the whole house in order that it may decide whether or not they are valuable.
Clause 6 introduces a compulsory feature. Men who are now in the three services are all volunteers. When they enlisted, whether it was last year or five, 15 or 20 years ago, they made a definite choice. They had the opportunity, wishing to serve their country, to become members of the army, the navy or the air force. Each officer and man made a deliberate choice as to the service in which he wished to devote some part of his life. Some of them deliberately chose a service in which to make a lifetime career. The government through this bill now intends to shift those officers and men from these three services into the Canadian Forces. The names of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Canadian Army will disappear.
These officers and men who chose to make a contribution to Canada as members of one of the three services will no longer have this choice. They will be shifted into the Canadian Forces and will no longer be able to take pride as members of the navy, army or air force. The government is now saying that they are now in the services and will remain as members of the renamed service without any choice in the matter.
I gave an example of what happened in the past during the committee hearings and I should like to repeat it on this occasion. It is drawn from the experience of September, 1939. On September 1, 1939 officers and men were attested, enlisted, and sworn into the Canadian field force. I speak from practical knowledge because I was acting as assistant to the adjutant of our regiment on that occasion. These officers and men became members of the Canadian field force. Within a short period of time the cabinet at Ottawa changed the name to the Canadian active service
April 24, 1967	COMMONS
force. The documents which had been prepared for the Canadian field force were destroyed.
All this has been recounted in the official history of the Canadian effort during wartime by Colonel Stacey. There was great wastage of time and money. New documents were issued in the name of the Canadian active service force and we were instructed throughout the army to re-enlist, reattest and swear in again the people who had been members of the Canadian field force. We went through all that reattestation.
The Canadian active service force provided only for service in Canada, so when the decision was reached that forces would be sent overseas-and it was reached very quickly-instructions came again from the cabinet through the Department of National Defence to the effect that everyone who had been sworn in to the Canadian active service force must be asked whether he wished to serve only in Canada or elsewhere in the world abroad. We had to go through the whole process once again. That happened in wartime when the officers and men were all volunteers.
In wartime it is conceivable that no one would object to a name being changed half a dozen times, from the Canadian field force to the Canadian active service force, the Canadian expeditionary force or anything of that nature. However, the government of that day took the stand that the officers and men, having specifically entered the Canadian field forces, should have the opportunity of saying whether they wanted to belong to a force of a different name.
That opportunity was given and the change was made. When it came to determining whether they would serve elsewhere than in Canada the government of the day decided the officers and men should have yet another opportunity to make a choice. When the several thousand who had been reattested into the Canadian active service force were asked whether they would serve outside Canada only a very small number declined to sign on for service abroad. The official history indicates that there were only about 500 all told who declined.
The point is that even in wartime the officers and men were given that choice. They were all volunteers and free citizens of this country. Our objection is that under clause 6 this opportunity is not to be given to the officers and men who are now in the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army, and the 23033-963
National Defence Act Amendment Royal Canadian Air Force. Without being reattested or sworn in, and without any choice whatsoever in this matter, once this bill is declared law these officers and men become members of the Canadian Forces.
I should like to move the following amendment to clear up this matter, and I am sure the Minister of National Defence, now that he has had time to think this over, will agree that this freedom of choice should be offered to the officers and men now in the services. Consequently I move:
That clause 6 be amended by adding thereto the following subclause:
(3) No officer or man who was a member of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army, or the Royal Canadian Air Force immediately prior to the coming into force of this part shall be enrolled in the Canadian Forces without his consent registered by reattestation.

Mr. Chairman, the matter raised in this amendment is most serious, one which will have the most far reaching and the longest lasting consequences of any in this bill. Unlike the minister I am not one who believes that the bill before us will provide the answer to our defence posture over the next 40 or 50 years. Indeed, I will be quite surprised if we do not find ourselves in the position of having to make further changes within the next two or three years.
However, it is to the amendment to clause 6 that I would like to address my remarks. Perhaps I will start by analyzing it as I understand it. It is quite clear when it says that officers and men who were members of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army or the Royal Canadian Air Force immediately prior to the coming into force of this part are, subject to the provisions of the National Defence Act, members of the Canadian Forces.
It says in effect, as the previous speaker pointed out, that this is compulsory. The word "conscription" has certain connotations, but I think it is an expression of the government's failure to recognize any moral responsibility whatsoever to serving officers and men in the three services.
The explanation of clause 6 is not very clear. The remarks of the minister concerning this clause leave much to be desired. All we know about clause 6 is that it is transitional. However, as I mentioned, a better explanation is needed. So strongly do I feel about this lack of information that in my opinion the government is open to the charge that its
April 24, 1967

National Defence Act Amendment failure to explain fully and properly the meaning of this clause is nothing more or less than a deliberate attempt to gloss over its very serious and far reaching implications.
I am not prepared simply to look at the word "transitional", to accept it and move on to the next clause. It is my hope that in the course of the remarks we may make on this clause the minister might give second thought to what is happening. As I read the clause and analyse it, I find the government is indeed saying to our 103,000 serving personnel "You are being transferred. You are fine, decent chaps; you know we have your best interests at heart, but just go along with our plan." In effect it says to them "Come along with us and we will look after you. The days of the identifiable services are gone, but have no particular fears about the new force. We will give you nothing at all to worry about. You will be there all right, but you will be there simply because we have decided. We will take care of you."
This is an abandonment of the very essence of the structure of our force, that is its voluntary nature. Every flag officer, every general, every air marshal and every commissioned officer is being told to burn his commission or toss it into the wastepaper basket. Since each was commissioned into only one of the three services, they are in effect being ordered to join the new force, and to accept something which is not part of the commission they originally accepted. Every officer and every man has been attested into the service of his choice, but he is now being attested into the service of the government's choice. Again I say this denies the voluntary nature and aspect of the structure of the Canadian armed forces.
First let us examine the voluntary aspects of their service. Each serving officer and man joined one and only one of the three services. He did so of his own free will after first having committed himself to a career for life in the Canadian forces and after having chosen which of the three services he wanted to join. He did this voluntarily. These men are in every sense of the word volunteers. Indeed, the officers volunteered to serve for life; that is for the length of time prescribed in the regulations for officers of the rank they would attain during their particular careers.
Each officer in any service on joining voluntarily had a different undertaking to the officers in the other services. This was the result of the free exercise of his choice. A naval officer decided to be different from an army


officer. Under the existing regulations naval officers who reach the rank of lieutenant commander have a career which continues until they reach the age of 45. An army major, whose rank is equivalent to that of the lieutenant commander, has a career which continues until he reaches the age of 49. An air force squadron leader, whose rank is equivalent to that of a major or lieutenant commander, serves to the age of 47 if he is on the flying list. Commanders, lieutenant colonels and wing commanders have careers which last until they reach the ages of 50, 49 and 49 respectively. Captains of the navy, colonels and group captains have careers which continue until they reach respectively the ages of 55, 51 and 51.
At one time the minister indicated that these careers were different. The fact is that each of the officers who joined voluntarily joined for a career which would last a certain length of time. I will repeat a word which I think is the key word in this context, namely "voluntary". They did so voluntarily. As far as I know no one as yet has been informed as to the length of the career which will apply to any particular rank in the new force.
The reason I introduce this problem is that serving officers and men are quite concerned about it. This legislation simply says to the whole of the officers' corps "Don't worry about it, old fellow. We will look after it. You no longer have anything to say about it."
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I come back to another point, the use of the word "transitional" in the explanation concerning clause 6. The explanation of the intent of the clause covers up the matter quite successfully. A cursory reading of the clause would, I suppose, leave a person in the same state as members of the committee were left, quite confused. What is important today is whether or not we have the right to permit this confusion, this uncertainty, to continue. What does the government mean and what does the minister mean by the use of the word "transitional"? Matters such as this must be cleared up so that the men who are being arbitrarily transferred will understand what it is they are transferring to, for what period of time and under what conditions.
If we pass this legislation without the consent of the officers and men, the bargain made with respect to the length of their careers, to which I referred earlier, will be broken. Alternatively, differences will be created which will most certainly cause resentment in rank levels where the different lengths of career
April 24, 1967

apply. This is a natural consequence of the failure to clarify these matter,i before this clause receives the approval of 'his committee. This again, is the underlying reason for the suggestion by the official opp isition that clauses 2 and 6 be allowed to stan 1 until the fall. This procedure would permit t \e departmental people time to come up with adequate answers and detailed explanation!; so that these men would know where they i e going and what is going to happen.
The fact that lieutenant commande s may have longer careers than hitherto and inajors may have shorter ones means you are p. aying around with the careers of officers \ 'hose lives have been voluntarily dedicated to a particular aspect of the service of Canada. This is not morally right, whether or not it is legal. While members of parliament may have the legal and constitutional right to do as they desire, there is a greater moral order, and sometimes I believe it would be wise for us to keep this in mind. We are doing something serious here, and this clause should be substantially amended.
I suggest that the amendment before us is a good one. If it is not made then not only the government but the House of Commons will have broken faith with these 102,000 men whose careers are governed by the promotion regulations in each of the three services. These regulations differ, but that is immaterial to the issue. Whether one service has a faster or slower method of promotion is not a matter of dispute. We do not argue about that at all because that was so in the past and must be so in the future. Promotion is geared to the requirements of the fighting environment. When you get to be even as old as I am you find it is more difficult to run uphill, and I am still fairly young. These factors must govern and because of that this area is not in dispute.
The point at issue is the fact that each of the services has separate promotional regulations. This is a fundamental thing, and I come back again to the freedom of choice. Before any man should be invited to accept a modified or unified system, he should have the new system fully explained to him and then be asked whether he will go along with it. If you transfer him without his consent you are compelling him to accept a different structure from the one for which he volunteered in the first place.
I believe this is the burden of the argument in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. The
23033-963 \
National Defence Act Amendment National Defence Act has provided, I think quite properly and fairly, that no officer or man can be transferred from one service to another without his consent except when the forces are on active service. This would be during a period of emergency as determined by parliament. The National Defence Act uses these words:
No officer or man shall without his consent be transferred from the regular forces to the reserve forces, or from the reserve forces to the regular forces, or from the service of the Canadian forces in which he has been enrolled to another service of the Canadian forces.
This is subject to the following exception:
An officer or man on active service, may for the period of such service, be transferred from the component of the service of the Canadian forces in which he has been enrolled to the same component of another service of the Canadian forces or from the reserve forces to the regular forces.
If clause 6 passes without amendment we will have shown a total disregard for the undertaking given to the officers and men who volunteered to serve Canada in the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force. This view was clearly expressed to the committee by one witness, and the reference is found at page 1050 of minutes of proceedings No. 20 for February 15, 1967. Rear Admiral William Landymore spoke at great length on this point but I shall not read his evidence into the record. I commend it to any member of the committee who is interested. This is one senior officer's opinion of the effect of the moral obligation which is left as a result of the amendment of this section of the National Defence Act.
I have listened to all the evidence in the committee and I have reread it on a number of occasions during the last two or three weeks. I cannot find anywhere in the evidence given by any of the officers, either presently serving or recently released, any argument whatever which effectively counteracts the argument advanced in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member. The minister has not attempted to prove that the government has neither legal nor moral obligations. I am sure he has accepted the fact there is a legal obligation, as the judge advocate general told the committee there was.
I believe that the minister recognizes the moral obligation whenever he is asked directly , but he has never done or said anything to counteract the meaningful amendment which is now before us. As I said earlier it has been
15240	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment glossed over as though it was unworthy of debate. We do not have the right to gloss over something which so radically affects the lives of the officers and men who have volunteered to serve and, if necessary, to give their lives in defence of this country. The judge advocate general, Brigadier Lawson, in his evidence before the committee concerning this clause pointed out that in his opinion it is law. We accept that, and I am not talking about the legality of it at all.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It may be of some interest to some people to pursue this matter in the courts of our country, particularly from a civil rights point of view. Mr. Chairman, I think the members of this committee should realize that unless the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre carries we will be asked to pass a law which brings in for the first time peacetime conscription in Canada. We are discussing a peacetime voluntary force in a democratic country and the government is now proposing conscription. There have been a couple of occasions in this nation's history when a major upheaval occurred over the conscription issue. Yet on both occasions conscription was justified because this country's very life was at stake and we were then involved in a very serious conflict. However, there is no war in sight today and no reason has been advanced on the part of the government for resorting to conscription.
What makes it even more reprehensible is that this conscription does not apply to a particular class of people who might be suitable for the armed services or whose presence in the services might be necessary for the preservation of this country. We are going to limit this conscription to those who are now serving in our armed forces simply because these people agreed with the government of Canada to serve in one or other of our forces as they exist today. Certainly anybody who looks at the situation in this light, which I think is the only fair light in which to look at it, must demand compelling reasons from the government for resorting to peacetime conscription of the members of our armed forces.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
How can the minister in all fairness conscript these men? Our men in the past have enlisted in the service of their choice as volunteers. If we take the navy as an example, they enlisted in the navy because they like naval traditions, naval life, the brotherhood of seafaring fighting men, and the kinds

I say there can be no mistaking what the minister is doing. He-when I refer to the minister I refer to the government-is changing the agreement that was made with these volunteers. The government in effect is saying: You have no choice. Is that fair? Should that sort of thing be necessary if the men, as the minister alleges, are enthusiastic about serving in his new armed force? The minister and General Allard say that the men will be proud and anxious to serve in this force. If that is so, why is there this discrimination? What is the minister afraid of? If the men are so enthusiastic, why is he afraid of giving them a choice?
When men have served 15 or 20 years of a 20 or 25-year career it is difficult for them to give up their pension rights and to find a suitable job in civy street. Why does the minister need clause 7 to reassure the men that in the new force they will perform duties similar to those they performed in the old force? The answer seems obvious. The minister seeks to conscript in peacetime a small number of men. The government is changing the terms of the employment contract unilaterally. I can only conclude that the minister has less confidence in this measure than have the members of this house or of the armed forces.
Furthermore, I am not satisfied that parliament has the legal right to do what it seeks to do. In my view this clause deals with civil rights. It has nothing to do with matters pertaining to the armed forces. Brigadier Lawson says that the men who enlist in our armed forces have no contract. That argument has little weight because in my view this clause deals essentially with a matter of civil rights. I know that military affairs come within the ambit of the federal government, but I also know that civil rights do not. They come within the ambit of the provincial governments. By passing this clause parliament may be infringing on the exclusive right of the provinces to deal with civil matters, civil rights legislation being an exclusive prerogative of the provincial governments. Dominion-provincial relations are important matters. Do we, therefore, wish to go ahead blithely and pass this clause if there is any question about provincial rights being involved?
The government is seeking to change a contract that the men entered into voluntarily and it is seeking to do so in peactime when

The situation the country would be confronted with would be that the members of the armed forces would not be subject to the provisions of this clause. Mr. Chairman, this is a most important clause and one which deserves the careful consideration of the committee.
First of all I should like to assure hon. members that these matters were given thoughtful consideration in the department and by the law officers of the crown. It has been suggested that the relationship between

DEBATES	April 24, 1967
officers and men and the crown is contractual in nature. It has long been held, both in the United Kingdom and Canada, that there is no bilateral contract between the Crown and an officer or man serving in the forces of the crown. Thus in 1896 it was said in a case in the United Kingdom:
-it has been laid down over and over again . . . that all engagements between those in the military service of the crown and the crown are voluntary only on the part of the crown and give no occasion for an action in respect of any alleged contract.
This case was applied in a Canadian judgment in 1921 where it was said that for both officers and men of the Canadian forces the engagements "are voluntary only on the part of the crown". The same decision was reached in 1940 when the Exchequer Court examined some nine previous cases.
In 1959, in an action for the recovery of pay and allowances, the Exchequer Court was called upon to determine whether anything in the National Defence Act had altered the previous non-contractual relationship between the crown and officers and men. In delivering judgment it was said:
-I think, that in construing the provisions of the National Defence Act I must apply the presumption that parliament, when enacting that act, did not intend to alter such a well established principle unless there be found therein language which in express terms or by clear implication leads to the conclusion that such an alteration was intended. An examination of the act satisfies me that it contains no such express terms or any language which clearly implies that such an alteration was intended.
It has also been suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite that this clause is not within the jurisdiction of parliament and that it comes into conflict with the constitution.
It has long been held that legislation by the government of Canada which properly relates to one of the heads of Section 91 of the B.N.A. Act is intra vires although it may affect the property and civil rights of individuals. Heading 7 of Section 91 is "Militia, Military and Naval Service, and Defence."
In 1958 the Supreme Court of Canada quoted with approval a judgment of the Privy Council in which it was said:
Most of the specific subjects in Section 91 do affect property and civil rights but, so far as the legislation of parliament in pith and substance is operating within the enumerated powers, there is constitutional authority to interfere with such rights.
A decision by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1962 is directly in point. In that case the Supreme Court was called upon to
April 24, 1967

decide whether a provision of the Exchequer Court Act, which provided that an officer or man of the armed forces was deemed to be a servant of the crown for purposes of establishing liability, was ultra vires as affecting property and civil rights. Part of the judgment reads as follows:
In my opinion, to declare the nature of the relationship existing between the crown and members of the armed forces for any or all purposes is legislation within the exclusive jurisdiction of parliament under head 7 and accordingly, intra vires. This does not depend, in my view, upon any such ground as that to do this is necessarily incidental to the powers of parliament under head 7: it is a direct dealing with the matter within such powers.
In considering this bill it must be presumed that officers and men join the service to serve their country, Canada. I do not think it is too unreasonable to assume that they will want to continue to serve Canada in the unified service. Nevertheless I think it can be argued that in view of the fundamental nature of the change proposed in merging three services into one, the officers and men should not, except in an emergency, be required to continue to serve against their will.
It was for this reason that I gave the standing committee on defence the assurance that the present policy in respect of releases would continue. I must admit that I have been impressed by the argument that it would be preferable to write the provision into the law rather than to rely on a statement of policy. I propose therefore, after we have disposed of the amendment now before us, to ask one of my colleagues to move the following as an amendment.
That clause 6 be amended by adding thereto subclauses three and four as follows:
6. (3) Notwithstanding anything in this act or in the National Defence Act and subject to subsection 4, where an officer or man was a member of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army or the Royal Canadian Air Force immediately prior to the day on which this act is proclaimed and, within two months after that day, makes application in writing to his commanding officer for his release, he is entitled, except in an emergency, to be released within six months after that day.
(4) Where a person while an officer or man has received university, advanced technical or aircrew training or education at public expense, his right to release under subsection 3 is subject to such conditions as may be prescribed in regulations made by the Governor in Council.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I am advised, Mr. Chairman, that there is some question of the amendment now before us being in order because, as I understand it, it is in exactly the same wording as an amendment moved by the hon. member for

National Defence Act Amendment Winnipeg South Centre in the committee, as recorded at pages 2371 and 2372. It is my understanding that a decision of the committee is binding on the house. Nevertheless, if you find that this amendment is in order I would ask the committee to defeat it and then I will ask one of my colleagues to introduce the amendment to which I have just referred and which I hope will be found generally acceptable.
Before I resume my seat, Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal briefly with the question of pensions which was raised by the hon. member for Halifax. First of all, there is no more money in the fund than is required to meet its obligations. As a matter of fact, hon. members will recall that in the estimates recently presented to the House of Commons the largest single increase, I think something in the order of $75 million for the fiscal year, was required to meet an actuarial deficit-I think only one fifth of the actuarial deficit -caused by increases in pay awarded to members of the armed forces last year.
It is true to say, therefore, that notwithstanding the size of the fund, the fund is committed to meet obligations on the basis of undertakings presently in force. It is a very generous pension fund, and I think quite rightly so because service in the armed forces is unlike service in many other fields of endeavour in that it requires the best of an officer or man during his most productive years. It is not unreasonable, therefore, that he should be treated accordingly by the people of this country. It was designed in order to keep officers and men in the forces once they had served for a reasonable period of time, and by and large it has been successful in doing this.
It is one of the provisions, I think, of most industrial and public pension plans, that after a certain period of service there is a definite advantage to the individual to remain in the organization or service in which he is employed. I believe one could raise a general question about the desirability of this kind of pension plan and the regidity that it introduces into our system, and perhaps the desirability of having much more portability than presently exists between different pension plans. However, at the moment we are looking at the problem strictly in the context of the legislation now before us, and in that context I think we must admit this bill does not change the circumstances under which the pension law was written in so far as its general application is concerned.

Servicemen leaving the service now are subjected to an actuarial reduction. They receive a smaller pension over a longer period of time, and this has been taken into account in determining the payments required to the fund from time to time, including the actuarial deficit to which I referred a moment ago. A suggestion was made to the effect that the actuarial reduction not apply. The result would be that a special benefit would be provided for people leaving the service. I think this would not be acceptable for one reason, according to my discussions with the officers and men of the forces, and that is that the people who would be most likely to take advantage of it are the pilots, engineers, lawyers and professional people whose training would be in the greatest demand in the civilian economy.
This problem has been freely discussed internally. We have come to the conclusion that the result of this kind of special treatment would not reflect directly our appreciation of the bill now before us but would reflect much more closely the opportunity available to individuals in the civilian economy. We have gone into this question very carefully over a long period of time to see whether or not there might be some relaxation in the present reduction at some senior levels. At the present time we have not been able to devise a policy which meets satisfactorily all the cases. We are still looking into it. I have not seen as yet a proposal which was not subject to very serious technical reservations.

While I am speaking of time I think it is going too far for people to announce to the public in one way or another that the time of the House of Commons spent on this bill has

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
That is all the time which has been spent on this bill and I wish that those who make announcements over the air or in the papers would be fair to the House of Commons and give the people of Canada the correct impression. We have not spent an excessive amount of time on this bill which is of major importance.
Clause 7 of the bill reads:
Except in an emergency, no officer or man who was a member of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army or the Royal Canadian Air Force immediately prior to the coming into force of this part shall, without his consent, be required to perform any duty in the Canadian Forces that he could not have been required to perform as a member of such service.
This clause recognizes something which we think should continue to be recognized, namely, that men have made a definite choice in entering one of the three services and should be given an opportunity to continue in the service of their choice. It is intended to protect people who are now in the three services from being required to perform duties outside those they might have been expected to perform in their present services. Obviously some such clause was necessary or the hierarchy of the department might transfer officers and men from navy to army or from army to air force who had no wish to serve in an altered capacity.
The very fact that this clause appears in the bill indicates that people who enter the defence forces after the passage of this measure will be subject to transfer among the branches of the service. Otherwise, why is it here? There will be two types of people in this service after this bill is passed, those who have already entered the army, the navy or the air force and those who enter the defence

force later. Though the minister has told us they will not be required to do certain things, they will obviously be subject to transfer with or without their consent. This may have a bad effect on morale or it may lead to unsatisfactory conditions.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
We had an example offered us which, frankly, I consider to be somewhat ridiculous. A pilot exercise was carried out in which two members of the army served on board a destroyer. The purpose was to see whether it would be satisfactory for somebody from the army to serve at sea. It all depends on the individual. Some people could serve as readily on land as at sea or in the air, but I do not think this pilot project proved anything at all. Nevertheless it is an indication that what is intended is that men who enlist in the future are going to be shifted, without any leave on their part, from one branch of the service to another or from one area to another. Even those whose enlistment earlier was in a special force-navy, army or air force-in an emergency will be moved about under the provisions of this clause.
The whole point of clause 7 is that it indicates the complete obliteration of the three distinct services. Yet in wartime there will still be activity at sea, separate and apart from land and air, there will still be activity in the air, separate and apart from land and sea, and there will still be activity on land, separate and apart from sea and air. This is taking place in Viet Nam at the present time. In the Vietnamese war there have been fights between fighter aircraft, and we had an example involving Israel and Syria just two weeks ago. But the minister has told us, "Oh no, all of this is in the past. All of this is old-fashioned. That is the way people used to do it in the olden days but now it is all different. No longer will there be clashes between air forces or clashes between fleets."
The strange thing is that other countries are still maintaining their fleets. They are building up their submarine fleets. For example, I do not know how an army is going to deal with a submarine 400 miles off the coast of Canada. It would appear to me you would have to have ships and airplanes to undertake that task, but the minister tells us that all of this is to be altered and nothing is to be done as it was done in the past.
I point out that under clause 7 the intention is quite obvious in an emergency to move the people presently in the services from one force to another, and it is also the intention
April 24, 1967	COMMONS
that when new people enlist in the future they will not have the privilege of those now in the separate services to select what they are going to do. They will be liable to be shifted back and forth. It is an undesirable clause.

I imagine that when this act comes into force there is going to be a clear distinction so long as there remains in the new force anyone who is carried over from the old forces. There will be two classes of citizens, so to speak, in the armed forces, and this clause is going to make sure that it will be a permanent distinction. One class of citizen will be the new members who are subject to any duty at all in the combined forces and the other class will consist of those carried over from the old forces who, when ordered to change duties, can say, "Just a minute; here are my duties." In other words, whether in the country generally or in the armed forces we have always tried to avoid making a distinction between the working or serving conditions of one citizen and another, but this is going to be perpetuated by this bill and perpetuated not just for the six months during which anybody now serving can get out of the services after the coming into force of the bill.
I have an idea why the minister included this provision. It is to reassure people that their conditions of service will not change that drastically, that it will be the same old job. It is to tell them that, just as the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra said, "Maybe you will have a new uniform but there will be no drastic changes and you had better stay on." This reveals the depths of the minister's fear of how shocking members of the present forces find unification, his fear of the amount of demoralization that has set in and his fear of the degree to which serving personnel are
National Defence Act Amendment going to abandon the unified force when they get a chance. So this provision is thrown out as a crumb to try to stem the tide of revulsion sweeping the forces against this bill.
It also points up very drastically some of the speeches which the minister and his supporters have made respecting the duties of the new force and the advantages of interchangeability even under integration, such as those claimed for the common training command. We have had some indications that training command is not working all that well. It has been discovered that there is not that much training in common among the three services, that specialization sets in so quickly that already, according to the evidence, there is real doubt that having one amalgamated training command has accomplished anything. Some testimony has been given that it is a waste of time and more expensive than an individual training command for each of the services. However, if the claimed great advantages of unification are going to be brought out, are going to be sold, then I suppose the minister had to sell the idea of interchangeability and training command was an illustration of it. All I can say is that this certainly makes a mockery out of his argument of interchangeability because if they have been trained in one service they cannot be required to perform in another. If we are going to get any advantages out of interchangeability, and we doubt there will be any in a realistic sense, then under the new set up only the new men who enter the force can be interchanged, according to the provisions of this clause.
However, I think this will not be the hindrance that it appears to be because the facts of military life are going to take effect, especially with reference to the phrase "without his consent." The classic army situation of asking for three volunteers, you, you and you, is not really so far removed from the truth. Volunteers in most instances are just picked at random or the sergeant may say to them, "You are going to do this, won't you?" That will be the extent of it and I think this is a beautiful illustration of the fallacy of some of the arguments used by the minister. It is a perfect illustration of the never-never-land in which the Minister of National Defence seems to live, in that it shows what he will do to try to sell this bill, what he will do to try to take the stink out of what he is doing to the armed forces and the extent to which he will go to make us believe everything is fine. But all this accomplishes is really nothing. The only worth of this provision will be shown if life

At this stage and subsequently on third reading we could delay the passage of this bill by a discussion on this point of importance. The defence of the realm is one of the prerogatives of the Crown which must be considered seriously. Just recently we witnessed a ceremony at which a representative of the crown was sworn in. During the course of that swearing-in ceremony it was obvious that the Queen's representative became the commander in chief of the military forces of Canada, the Canadian defence forces. In view of the grave responsibility which rests upon the representative of the crown in this regard it is essential that a minister at some stage-this would have to be done before third reading-indicate to the House of Commons that the consent of the Governor General has been obtained in respect of this fundamental change in this area of his responsibility.

On the other hand, under our system of a constitutional monarchy with a parliament consisting of the crown, the House of Commons and the Senate, anything that infringes upon the prerogatives of the crown should be considered carefully. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to deliver a few remarks on the second reading of this bill on behalf of the minister, who was on his way to fulfil a speaking engagement prior to our being advised that the bill would be coming up for consideration this evening. The absence of the minister is entirely unavoidable, and I should like to make these remarks on
Occupational Training
his behalf. I do not believe anyone expected the unification bill would be disposed of this afternoon, after such a lengthy debate.
Mr. Speaker, the bill we are to discuss this evening is not new in principle, to members of this house. The policy on which it is based was made clear by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) last October. Essentially, what the bill does is to give the government of Canada power to buy various kinds of training for Canadian workers. Hitherto, we have not done this. We have reimbursed the provinces for a part of the costs that they incurred in providing training. The change puts us in a more positive role. It makes us responsible for seeing that training responds to the needs of the economy. But I want immediately to make it very clear that, in doing this, we are not violating provincial jurisdictions. We represent the consumers of training. We are enabling the demand for training to be effective.
To serve its purpose, training must be provided in the occupation in which the individual will be able to find employment suited to him. We propose to pay for that training. There is no thought of our doing the training. The bill of course does not provide for that. It simply makes us the financial agents of all the hundreds of thousands of Canadian workers whose future earnings are dependent on more training, but who do not have the resources to invest in the training at the time they need it.
There is no doubt about the economic need for the program. Canada's demands for skilled workers must very largely be met by tapping the reservoir of able but untrained people in our labour force. That is the principal way to meet the skilled manpower shortages which hold back our industrial growth. The bill is directed toward those goals. It is not designed to compete with provincial education and training systems. It is not to provide cultural betterment, or to help people go to university. Those are vital matters, but they are not what this program is about.
Every day technological change robs old skills of their value. Men and women who were once adequately trained find that they cannot compete in our increasingly technical world. Since 1949, for instance, over half a million farmers have left Canadian agriculture. Very few of them left with the skills that other industries needed. In our new economy the number of people who will have only one occupation during their lives is very

April 24, 1967
Occupational Training
small. But retraining people whose jobs are disappearing is only part of the task; we must also train the adults who earlier could not get the training that people need today. Even compared with ten years ago, school systems have been greatly expanded and diversified. They provide today's secondary school graduates with much more of the knowledge needed to earn one's way in the world.
But that has been no help to the great majority of people who are now working. The opportunities were not there during their youth. The training that will be financed under this legislation must meet the practical needs of a wide range of mature adults and it must frequently utilize techniques different from those normally employed in the training of youth. We cannot realistically ask a mature adult to return to school for an extended period of time; we must have accelerated courses which will do the job as quickly as possible. Adults want to work at a job; training is a route to that goal, not a goal itself.
The core of a successful adult training program is the ten months skill course. The provinces run a wide range of such courses, and we can expect that this range will widen further as the program expands. But workers all too often have forgotten-or never received-their basic training in arithmetic, scientific and linguistic skills. When this background is necessary for a skill course that a worker wants to take, we will pay for it. But the intent of the program is not extended educational training. The basic upgrading is simply a means to the objective, which is occupational training.
The individual courses that will be financed for adults will extend from a week to a year, depending on what they want and need. A man may need, and will be able to get, a one year upgrading course followed by a one year skill course. But this will not be a lifetime limit. A basic premise of the program is that our manpower needs shift over time. A man who must pursue several occupations during his working life may need training for each one.
It is not, of course, enough to make the proper kind of training available. Adults who have economic responsibilities need income during training. Those people who have been members of the labour force-for the past three years, or for one year if they have dependants-will be eligible for allowances to let them take training.
Eligibility for payment of training costs will require only that a person be one year above the school leaving age and have been

out of school for one year. Even the last condition will be waived for apprentices. But it would not be fair to give people who lack adult responsibilities the allowances designed to let people discharge those responsibilities. We would not wish, by offering .these allowances, to induce young people to drop out of school and take short term adult training when more high school training or a technological institute course is what they most need.
There will be no means test for allowances and a person need not be unemployed to qualify. These allowances are an income substitute to let people take training. They are not a form of relief. The allowances will initially be between a minimum of $35 and a maximum of $90 a week, varying with the number of dependants a man has and the general level of earnings in his province or region. The maximum scale will be $35 for a person who supports only himself, $55 for a person with one dependant, $65 if there are two dependants, and $75 if he has three or more dependants. In addition, a person who must leave his home town to take training will get up to $15 weekly to compensate for the extra expense. This is a total of $90 per week, or approximately $390 monthly.
e (8:10 p.m.)
We will seek provincial advice and agreement on the appropriate level of the allowance we use in each province. If a province wishes, we will be willing to use different scales in different parts of a province to better reflect variations in the level of earnings.
The bill provides that, starting on July 1, 1968, the allowance limits will be escalated each year in line with the increase in average hourly earnings in manufacturing. Over the last available five-year period this index has gone up by an average of 3J per cent each year. The scales used in each province and the amount for each dependant will be adjusted at the same time as the national limits.
An essential aspect of allowances for adults is prompt and regular payment. I should therefore mention one detail that is provided for in the regulations. Canada Manpower Centres will be able to advance $25 to those who need it to help tide them over during their first week of training. Most adult training courses will be provided by provincial or municipal authorities. Of course, we will deal only with the province, which will make its arrangements with the municipalities.
The bill means that, when we enrol a adult in a publicly operated training course,
April 24, 1967

we will pay the cost of putting on the course and we will pay an amount to compensate the province for the capital and interest charges on the buildings and equipment that are used. We will pay a fair share of the provincial overheads involved in providing general administration for the courses. We will have an interim payment system to ensure that the provinces get a steady flow of cash to meet their expenses. The financial settlement at the end of the year will be based on the actual costs of training.
The bill lays it down that we will purchase training from the province when it is available. But if the province agrees that it does not have the course a man needs near where he lives, we will be able to pay for training in a privately operated course. In this case we will negotiate a fee, not above the usual level, with a private training school.
The bill also provides for the purchase of training in industry. A man who is employed should not be forced to quit his job in order to get training. In most firms, workers accumulate seniority and pension rights. To sacrifice these rights to take training would frequently mean to abandon the only security a man has.
The training we will pay for in industry is the same kind that is available in public institutions. It would be easy to record a vast increase in training if we offered to pay for the kind of on-the-job training that new employees get in most firms. But that would not be an economic use of public funds.
What we will pay industry to do is the type of training that it now does all too infrequently. That is the classroom type of training that the provinces provide to people who are not employed. But in industry "classroom" becomes a rather elastic term. One of the great advantages of industry as a training ground is that it already has the modern equipment thar people must use in their jobs. A "classroom" in industry can be a part of a factory floor. It is the equivalence of the training given in public institutions that counts, not whether people sit at desks.
Although nearly all firms routinely provide on-the-job practice to new workers, only one manufacturer in four gives even one day's formal training to any of his workers. This is not because firms fail to recognize the need. It is because general training is often uneconomic for the individual firm. The workers who would benefit frequently leave for jobs with other firms, so that the company that does classroom training may help its competitors as much as itself.
Occupational Training
Accordingly the bill recognizes a public obligation to pay for classroom training in industry. We must see that training is good business for the individual firm as well as for the individual worker. But we will not pay all of the firm's costs of training. The company will derive real benefit from the trained workers who do stay with it. Therefore it is sufficient to pay for the direct costs a firm incurs in training its workers; the firm will need to contribute the use of its facilities and equipment.
The biggest of the direct costs is the wages the firm pays workers while they are in training. We will reimburse the firm for most of these wages. We will calculate the proportion of the normal working week that is devoted to training. That proportion will be applied to the maximum training allowance or to the normal weekly wage, whichever is the lower.
There is one situation in which the bill provides payment for training in industry of a kind that is not provided in public institutions. When a technological change is going to displace established long-term employees at the same time as the company needs new people to run the automated equipment, we will be able to pay for on-the-job training in order to encourage the firm to retrain its older employees for the new jobs rather than hire outsiders.
Not all the training by industry will be done in factories. Sometimes it is more efficient for workers to take time off to go to nearby provincial institutions, and the bill provides for payment in such cases. Training need not be full time.
Thus the bill makes it possible for training to be provided in various ways to meet different situations. The training can be in courses operated by provincial or municipal authorities, private training schools, or employers. The courses can be full time, part time, evening, correspondence, or even by T.V. We hope that the provinces, which are improving adult training methods, will continue their experimentation.
For the individual Canadian this bill means that federal services will be available to help him decide what training course will benefit him most, to pay for the course; and to pay him an allowance to maintain an income while training.
The vast majority of these adults will be referred to provincial courses by a Canada Manpower Centre. The manpower counsellor will help people to find out what they can best do. Many people already have solid and

April 24, 1967
Occupational Training
marketable skills, and the need is to find the right job lor them. Sometimes a man has an adequate skill but there is no market for it locally; if so, the counsellor will be able to offer a mobility grant for a permanent or exploratory move to another town where the skill can be utilized. Frequently, however, the need is for training. When this is what the man wants and needs, we will be able to pay for it.
A rather different arrangement will be made for apprenticeship training. Thousands of apprentices, engaged in three or four year programs, take a six or eight week provincial course every year. These apprentices are not in need of counselling; they are already in a program which will give them a solid trade. They will be able to proceed directly to training.
Similarly, we will not ask people being trained in industry to march en masse into a manpower centre. If they wish it we will, of course, provide individual counselling before or after training. But in the main our officers will determine simply that the prospective trainees are qualified and that there is a healthy market for the skills to be taught; there is no need for us to duplicate the work which is carried on by company personnel directors.
I am afraid that we must face the fact that there are today more adults who need training than the system can handle this year. We cannot expect to provide training immediately to all who could benefit from it. At first we will have to select the people who need the training most. Obviously an unemployed man should get priority if he is able to benefit. The general criteria will be the size of the income increase that the training will give the man, his ability to absorb the training, and his determination and ability to put it to use afterwards. In all cases we must look to see that there will be a long run demand for the skills; there is no point to training a man for unemployment.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I do not mean that every trainee will always get a job right away after training. We must face the fact that training helps to fill demands for skilled people; it does not itself create that demand. Training can shift people from occupations generally in low demand to occupations generally in high demand, but it does not create a particular job.
In recent years all our labour markets have grown tighter. I am confident that properly managed policies can keep the economy run-
ning at a high pace. But even if there is a temporary decline in demand, our training efforts should not falter; they are the way to save the individual from being a permanent victim of recession.
There are a few other features of the bill that I should mention at this stage. When we pay for provincial courses, we will be including an amount to cover the costs of capital and interest involved. The bill recognizes that not all provinces can readily borrow the money they need to construct training facilities. We will be able to make loans to construct and equip adult training centres. Interest on these loans will be only fractionally above the long term interest rate that the federal government must pay, and it will be below the rate at which the provinces could normally borrow on the market. Our fees to the provinces for training adults will be the source of interest and capital payments on these loans.
Also, of course, the phase-out of the old T.V.T. capital payments may be used by the provinces for increasing their capacity to train adults.
Approximately $550 millions in grants will be available to cover 50 per cent or 75 per cent of the costs of construction of many projects, and a province can borrow the rest of the money for an adult centre from us if it wishes.
Another need is teachers. Indeed, one of the skills which is most in demand today is the skill possessed by an experienced tradesman or technician who has also learned how to teach adults. So long as technical and vocational teachers continue to be in short supply, our counsellors will be able to refer men and women who possess the necessary technical skills to courses which will train them in the art of passing on those skills. Thus the program will pay to train the trainers.
If the provinces are to experiment with new ways of teaching adults, and if we are to develop better ways of matching training with our emerging manpower needs, we must have research.
We propose therefore to co-operate with the provinces in paying for research which is concerned with developing new ways to teach adults and with designing courses to fit adult needs. The research which is done to better the training of adults will also contribute toward improving the training provided in secondary and post-secondary schools.
I might add that we have already taken some highly significant steps to foster development of more suitable methods for adult
April 24, 1967

training. Our pilot adult training projects will shortly be getting under way. These projects are frankly experimental. They are 100 per cent financed by the federal government but they will be run by independent boards appointed jointly with the provinces. The boards will be given complete freedom, within their budgets, to experiment in the development of advanced and accelerated methods of adult training.
Hon. members will recall previously when there was some discussion that they asked for an indication of the magnitude of the expenditures which we anticipate and the number of adults we expect in training. It is very difficult to estimate our expenditures this year, partly because of the transitional arrangements with the provinces. Capital phase-out payments will probably be about $120 millions. We expect that training costs, including other transitional payments, will come to about $110 million.
Future expansion must depend on the needs and on the resources available. At present there are 288 publicly operated centres which train adults. The adult enrolment at the beginning of the year was 65,716. We expect that in this fiscal year a total of about 120,000 people will receive adult occupational training in public institutions. The number will increase considerably in subsequent years. Until we have had more experience, I would not wish to predict the pace of the increase. But I would expect that in the foreseeable future the number of people trained in a year should rise to about 5 per cent of the labour force-which at present would mean over 350,000 persons.
I believe that we are moving into economic circumstances that make adult training on this large scale essential. It is the way to make our economy fully productive. It is the way to make the door to the affluent society open for the individual Canadian.
This bill creates the machinery to respond to the urgency of the need for adult training. I believe that the benefits, to our economy and to our people, will be very great indeed.
This bill has been waiting for some time to be considered; it has been waiting while hon. members discussed the unification bill. In order that the government should not be deprived of the opportunity to provide training, it has been necessary, since April 1, to supplement the program by regulations under the authority of interim supply.
During this period certain criticism has been made in press reports which may be
Occupational Training
causing some confusion as to the facts. I would like, therefore, to end by repeating this statement on the essential facts that the minister made yesterday:
Many more Canadians now have the opportunity for retraining for a better job. This is the effect of the program. It means that every person in Canada who has been out of school for more than a year can benefit from retraining. The federal government will pay the whole cost of occupational training for anyone who will be able as a result to do a better job. This includes immigrants equally with long-term residents and citizens.
The new program replaces previous arrangements under which retraining was available only to workers who were unemployed or who fitted various special categories.
In order to take training most adults must be provided with an income while training. This is fully covered in the federal program by means of training allowances. These allowances are a minimum of $35 a week and considerably more, up to $90 a week, for workers with dependants to support.
The only restriction on these allowances is that they are not to be used to compete with the school system. They are designed for retraining, not to make training a substitute for school. Therefore, to qualify for allowances as well as free training, a trainee must either have dependants or have been working or seeking work for the past three years.
These facts were made public in October at the last federal-provincial conference. It was made clear that there was nothing to prevent any province from offering allowances to younger people without dependants, if it so wishes.
From the start, the new program will train at least as many workers as the former program did. The federal government is providing larger funds, and as the provinces provide more facilities, an increasing number of people will benefit.
I believe I have nothing further to add at this time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
May I say at the outset that we endorse what the parliamentary secretary has said as to the importance and urgency of this bill. As a matter of fact I think the record of the last two or three weeks will show that on several occasions we in the opposition tried in vain to get this item moved to the head of the order of business because we felt it was certainly much more urgent than the question of unification.
As we move into a new area of business, in the light of past experience with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mar-chand) who has shown he can accept suggestions and advice even from the opposition benches, I am sure we can proceed with much more efficiency and make much better progress than was evident in connection with the unification bill.

Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) introduced the resolution preceding this Bill No. C-278 on March 3 last, I had the opportunity to congratulate him and the government on this step forward.
On behalf of my colleagues, I have no hesitation in renewing my encouragement and I trust that the minister will take into due consideration our few remarks during this debate.
Any discussion concerning the occupational training of adults affords us the welcome opportunity to look fully into this problem of prime importance for the development and progress of society with regard to future opportunities, challenges and needs.


In the course of his remarks on March 3, the minister stated:
This new program is an integral part of a national manpower policy whose basic purpose is to bring economic opportunity within the reach of Canadian workers.
This all sounds very good. It seems to imply that the government is ahead of the game and reaching forward with benevolent policies. I believe, though, that we must consider this as being the government's side of the story only. It was surely not the good heartedness of the government, its deep concern for the well-being of Canadian workers, which inspired the minister of manpower to prepare and introduce this bill. I believe that hon. gentlemen on the front benches opposite, as the government, and we, as members of parliament, are forced to consider this action as a matter of cold, economic necessity.
Our best economists and social scientists have long been urging all institutions responsible for this country's social development as well as for its educational policies to face the fact that as Canada emerges as a modern industrial society our old occupational structures must change, and change fast, if we are to remain competitive in the international market and retain the benefits of an affluent society.
Mr. Speaker, a technological society cannot come into its own or even develop satisfactorily unless opportunities are provided for all segments of the society to obtain higher and modern education. I will not attempt, for the time being, to invade the sacred area of formal education-I should like to remain in politics for a little while longer-but I am concerned by a forecast made by one scientist that in a highly industrialized society, one constantly in an atmosphere of progress and change, a man must anticipate four or five occupational changes in the course of a lifetime. Four or five such changes implies as many periods of readjustment or retraining.
It is difficult to deny or to ignore such a forecast, and this makes our responsibility as a parliament for finding forceful answers to these questions even greater than it would normally be. That is why we are anxious to see the present measure come forth for consideration in spite of weaknesses which it contains, weaknesses which can possibly be ironed out later.
In his introductory speech of March 3, the minister referred to the training allowances
April 24. 1967

act which provided greatly needed opportunities for training unemployed workers, together with a measure of financial assistance. This was, and remains a progressive piece of legislation and parliament had no hesitation in seeing it through, because it was timely. However, this should not prevent our calling attention to certain weaknesses which have shown up since its inception-weaknesses which might be avoided in the present case. I refer specifically to the fact that approximately one third of the budgeted amounts were not used. The people for whom the bill was enacted did not respond. Why?
I believe the simple answer is that the government and the department of manpower just did not bother to do the necessary research and prepare the groundwork so as to make sure that the measures they brought forward were those best suited to answer the needs. The same considerations apply to the measures proposed in Bill C-278. I believe no program of this magnitude and consequence should be put forward for enactment unless it has been preceded by an extensive and expert research program. No act which will affect millions of people in the days ahead and which will cost millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money can be accepted by this house unless the minister can explain on a basis of facts-dry facts and figures-that an effective adult education program is under way. The public must be made aware of its advantages. The interest of the people involved must be awakened so that they appreciate the value and necessity of further education, as well as the economic advantages of retraining to meet the requirements of an industrialized society.
When I mention the need for a research program I do not mean political research to find out what sounds best for the purpose of catching votes, but scientific research into ways and means of accomplishing specific ends.
Nowhere in his introductory remarks did the minister indicate, much less prove, that such a research program into adult education had been carried out. Yet without it we are heading for possibly failure. We have been given no indication that the minister or his department have done their homework before sitting the exam. The example is appropriate at this time of the year when our children are preparing for the year-end tests. We constantly remind them that if they do not do their homework they cannot expect promotion. By the same token, if we do not tell our children just how important a good education is, the
Occupational Training
number of drop-outs will inevitably increase. How can we expect to build a great society or, in the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), "a good society", on the basis of an increasing number of drop-outs or, in the present case, of adults who do not respond to these training opportunities. The government must have learned from its experience in connection with the training allowance act that human desires and needs cannot be met, nor human interest be awakened, by money or financial assistance alone. Yet most of the parliamentary secretary's remarks tonight centred around the idea of paying and paying for services.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
We will influence and interest people if we first convince them of the values and needs of education and training, through proper methods of communication between those who direct the economy, the planners, and those who execute, the workers. We know for instance that quite a number of federal departments are involved and have spent millions of dollars on research programs on social development. Just to mention a few, they are the Department of Forestry and the ARDA program, the Department of Industry, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and presumably, at least I hope so, the Department of Manpower and Immigration.
Has there been any co-ordination between these various programs? Have they gone their separate ways? Has one department relayed its information to the other? Has manpower sought out relevant information from the other departments? Have interested groups been consulted systematically to investigate real employment opportunities? Is there a followup program already prepared to shore up possible weaknesses or shortcomings if something goes wrong or if, once again, there is no public response?
I think, Mr. Speaker, we all agree that we must have the answers to these questions before we can be expected to support the bill. More questions come to mind. How many jobs must be filled? Some figures were given tonight. How were they arrived at? Are they guesswork, or scientific in their content? How many candidates are expected in the first, second and third years? Where are the jobs located? Are they concentrated in urban areas, or will people be directed to new areas where new opportunities are needed? Are the

April 24. 1967
Occupational Training
people involved willing to go where the opportunities are before they undertake retraining? Have these people said so, or is the department guessing again?
Have the provinces shown any response to the federal government's offer to lend money over a period of 30 years for building training facilities? What happens to those loans if facilities are put to other use after five or ten years? What is meant by the phrase "private training facilities" contained in the minister's speech of March 3? It is hoped, indeed it is essential that this information be given to members of the house before we are asked to approve Bill 278.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that the minister is particularly concerned with any form of discrimination, no matter where or how it is expressed. I would sincerely hope that training opportunities as implemented or developed through the Canada manpower centres will not be taxed with or accused of such discrimination because of poorly defined policies.
Another consideration which must occupy our minds in studying this bill is the very evident misunderstanding which already seems to exist between the provincial and federal governments as to the effects of discontinuing existing programs in favour of the present provisions in this bill. The case has been very clearly spelled out in an editorial feature in the Globe and Mail of Saturday, April 22, under the title "The Retraining Row," with appropriate subtitles such as, "Queens Park Points a Finger at Ottawa," and "Ottawa Points a Finger Right Back." I imagine, Mr. Speaker, other hon. members will draw your attention to this article so I shall not put it into the record, although it would be well worth the while and the time.
Basically, the problem that this controversy underlines is the fact that the manpower department could easily lose sight of the fact that, independently of this or that argument, the basic concerns here are manpower, the national economy and the industrial society. All of these are federal concerns which must be met. No exchange of letters will settle that, and I urge the minister to get into these discussions, personally and immediately, with the provincial authorities. Let his successful experiences of the past as a hard but sensible negotiator come to the rescue, because one thing is certain: If this plan does not work, whatever the reason, he will have to answer for it not only to himself and to his government but also to the population as a whole.
