speechtext:
Listening to the parliamentary secretary this evening I was dismayed that I could detect no consideration on the part of the government for the objections to the basic principles contained in this bill which were enumerated when the bill was debated last March. I was one of the members of the joint committee dealing with the white paper on immigration which heard representations about the shortcomings in the white paper, pointed out by individual members in the committee and by organizations from one end of Canada to the other in hearings which lasted for many weeks. Members of the committee were happy, and complimented the minister on the fact that he was broadminded enough to listen to the representations that were made and to study them. Many of those representations pointed out defects in the white paper, and last week the minister came to the committee with a statement which in effect rewrote major provisions in the white paper, substituting for them much more sensible and humane provisions.
I too complimented the minister. That is why I find it hard to understand why he, who was able to be realistic and specific in reassessing the principles he had enunciated in the white paper, and who was able to change his mind and, in effect, propose a modified policy, should now tonight, through the parliamentary secretary, make a speech in which not one principle enunciated by him last March 3 has been changed, and in which not one of the detailed objections have been met. More important, Mr. Speaker, I find it hard to understand why none of the objections by the various provincial governments, which have had a great deal of experience with manpower training programs, has been dealt with by the parliamentary secretary. It is as though nothing has happened in the last few months; as though none of the objections had any weight. It is as though nobody knows anything but the minister and a few of his top officials and, as a result, the suggestion is that we are to go ahead and accept all the provisions of this bill whether we like them or not, or whether the provinces and the educators like them or not. Apparently the minister and a few other key officials have all the answers.
I want to reiterate what we said on March 3, that in our opinion this division which the government makes between education, as the government calls it, and manpower training, is a completely fictitious one. It is a division which will lead to untold and incalculable difficulties. I can only assume, Mr. Speaker,
April 24, 1967

that what we have here is the working out to the Nth degree of the principle which seems to have been adopted by the government, I suppose at the suggestion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau), that Ottawa must not infringe on fields which are the responsibility of the provinces; and if one province objects, then Ottawa cannot make any arrangements with the other provinces.
This is a completely fallacious position and one which will lead from one difficulty to another. After all, Mr. Speaker, if the provinces are in the field of technical and vocational training today-and I think it is good that they are-it is because the former Conservative government brought in a technical vocational training act in 1961 under which more than $600 million was given in capital grants to the provinces by the federal government.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
As a result of this program there are in virtually every province in Canada effective technical and vocational training programs. Having co-operated with the federal government in a program which was urged on them by the federal government it is not surprising that the provinces not only have gone into these programs but have made plans to expand and continue them. The fact is, and I do not think there can be any question about it, that the provinces were met at the last federal-provincial conference by a unilateral decision on the part of the federal government to get out of the technical vocational program field. I should like to read a few lines from the statement at that conference by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), where he said:
We are determined to get out of shared cost programs in education ... For us to be involved in the school system in the name of technical and vocational training inevitably introduces distortions ... Increasingly your decisions-
Meaning the decisions of the provinces.
-as to what to do are influenced by a natural desire to get as much as possible out of the programs of which we will pay 50 per cent.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the federal government which encouraged the provinces to get into the technical vocational training field should be criticized for having framed that program. Indeed the federal government should be commended for this, because I think it is a very great advance in educating the young people of this country in
Occupational Training
ways which they will find useful. Later in the same statement the minister said:
So, unless you are prepared to argue that we should have the permanent influence on your programs that shared-cost arrangements give us, I suggest that you must accept the principle of our withdrawal.
On March 3 I said, and I now say again, that this withdrawal is a disaster for the people of Canada, for the young people who wish to leave school, and for those who will need to be retrained. I believe that rather than get out of the shared program in the field of technical and vocational training the federal government should expand its role. We have this unilateral decision to get out and as a result of that we have the draft of a program, the regulations for which most of us until recently and some of us until today have not had an opportunity to look at. I am informed that it is true not only in respect of the province of Ontario but also the province of Manitoba that the entire decision to get out-not only the principle, but the details of the program which is now before us and which will be carried on as a result of the implementation of this bill-was worked out unilaterally by the federal government and by the department of manpower. I am informed there were no consultations with the provinces. Because of the fact that the province of Ontario is the largest and most industrially oriented province, and I am quite sure has the most successful technical and vocational training program in the country, it is not surprising, as reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail, that the minister of education of the province of Ontario asked to see the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to discuss the new program, the details in respect of it, and some of the problems which will arise and which are arising as a result of the change in the program.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration, however, could not find the time to meet with the minister of education of the province of Ontario. Well, I do not suppose it is my function to tell the minister what his job is, but I think that had he spoken at a few less Liberal party meetings and had met with the minister, we might have been a little further ahead. I understand that the Canadian Association for Adult Education asked the minister for a meeting so that they could discuss this matter with him. I believe they have a technical and vocational committee which is interested. They could not arrange a meeting with him. He was too busy.

April 24, 1967
Occupational Training
The result of this is that in every province questions are being asked. Rather than expose us to the dry, dull dreary statement which the parliamentary secretary gave us tonight, it would have been better had the minister dealt with the suggestions which are listed in an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of Saturday, which was referred to by the previous speaker from the official opposition. It may be that those objections are not correct, but the article in the Globe and Mail of last Saturday and its article of last Thursday quoted officials of the federal department, who are supposed to implement the program, as saying completely contradictory things in respect of how this program will work.
I should like to quote from the Globe and Mail of April 20:
L.F.D. Coulson, Ontario assistant director, Canada Department of Manpower and Immigration, admitted the regulations were a "semi-fait accompli" and that there was confusion over them.
He said the manpower department would give an extremely broad interpretation to what constituted three years continuous work experience.
He said it would include a housewife of three years.
In other words, a woman who had not worked but who had been a housewife for three years, in the opinion of Mr. Coulson, would be able to participate in the retraining grant. The article goes on to say, however:
An Ottawa spokesman for the department said a housewife's duties would not likely be considered labour force experience.
If the officials in the department do not know what the program is and how the regulations will be implemented, is it any wonder that there is consternation, and indeed that there is a panic among the provincial authorities who have been operating the manpower training programs since 1961. What are some of the difficulties? I shall deal with a few of the many difficulties which I am sure will face us when we are dealing with the bill clause by clause, and even more so when we study the regulations which have been implemented and which, as stated by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), were brought about in a pretty slippery way.
What do we find in the new regulations? The key point is that they exclude from the allowances any person under age 17 and any single person over 17 with fewer than three years working experience. I suggest that this is complete nonsense. We might take the example of a person who leaves high school. I am not too concerned about whether he
[Mr. Orlikow.J
finishes high school and receives a diploma, whether the existing curriculum in the high school does not fit his needs, or that he leaves for reasons of his own. Surely it does not make sense that we should say to such a youngster who is 17, 18 or 19 years of age that he cannot attend one of these manpower retraining centres now, that he cannot receive a living allowance now, and that he must go out and find work such as sweeping floors, or do anything-even be unemployed.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
According to the provisions of this bill one must be unemployed for a substantial period of time before being eligible. During this time of unemployment these young individuals may become married and start to raise families. At that time, when they are living on their own with their families, we then all of a sudden become happy to allow them to attend our retraining centres. Then we must not only pay for the retraining, we must pay a living allowance. What earthly sense can there be in that kind of artificial approach?
Surely what we must do is encourage everyone who wants to increase his ability to perform a job which requires a skill to do so as quickly as possible. By imposing this kind of penalty we are being unfair to the young people concerned. As a result of this attitude yve will suffer a great economic loss in this country.
This bill is discriminatory against women. The present government has appointed a royal commission to study the status of women. Many women who married early have children and have not been part of the working force for many years. At the age of 35 or 40 their children have become more or less independent and they may wish to go back to work. Under the provisions of this bill women who have not been in the working force will not qualify for admission to our retraining centres. That is not only a disadvantage to the country, because of a waste of potentially productive capacity, it is discriminatory against those individuals.
When we reach our clause by clause study of this bill we must consider carefully that portion relating to training programs in industry. I do not criticize industrial training programs, indeed I suggest they are not now numerous enough. Industry should be encouraged to participate in those schemes which will upgrade their employees' skills. Nothing in these provisions spells out the type of program in respect of which grants will be made by the federal government, nor do they
April 24, 1967

indicate the amount of money envisaged by the government to be allocated toward the cost of these industrial programs. It is conceivable that several large companies, and I think specifically of the railway companies, Air Canada and Bell Telephone, may devise programs which could use up the total amount of federal government money allocated under the provisions of this bill for the coming year. I am not suggesting that would be wrong in principle, but nothing is set out in the bill, and nothing has been said by the parliamentary secretary, which would indicate the relationship between the amount of money available and the number of programs involved for this type of program, and the total for all programs.
I was surprised that the parliamentary secretary, who represents a constituency in the city of Hamilton, with a large number of immigrants did not deal with the subject matter of concern expressed by the province of Ontario, the city of Toronto and other provinces. This matter was referred to by the Toronto chairman of the metropolitan board of education in an article which appeared in today's Toronto Globe and Mail. He took very strong exception to what he considers to be a clear indication in this bill, that the immigrants that have come to Canada in large numbers, and who will be coming to Canada during the next year or two, will be very sharply curtailed so far as their right to attend these training centres is concerned. This is true because of the requirement that individuals must have been available for employment for a period of three years prior to their qualification for inclusion in this program.
The board of education in Toronto is spending $1,500,000 this year to teach immigrant adults and children to speak English. In light of that effort by the city of Toronto and similar efforts on the part of cities such as Winnipeg, which I happen to represent, it seems very strange that the federal government should embark on a program which will not be available to those individuals who require training. Obviously that is the case, unless there are regulations in respect of this bill which members of this house and officials of the provinces have not seen or understood.

speechtext:
I wonder why the parliamentary secretary finds it necessary to get up at 10 minutes after 9 p.m. on Monday, April 24, to tell a backbencher from the city of Winnipeg that this has been known for months, in light of the fact that provincial officials have been trying for some time to discuss this matter with the federal Minister of Manpower and Immigration. If this fact has been known for months, why is it that the Ontario provincial minister of education has not known about it? Why is it that the chairman of the Toronto metropolitan board of education has not known about it, and why did the minister have to issue a press statement yesterday apprising interested parties of this fact? Why were these things not discussed in detail with provincial officials?
Some people have suggested that the New Democratic party developed the expression "co-operative federalism". In any event the government has adopted this phrase as an expression of its policy. In spite of that fact this federal government states that this is what it intends to do and the provinces must accept it or leave it. To my way of thinking co-operative federalism in this field suggests that the federal government should say that this is what it thinks ought to be done, and then ask the provinces to discuss the situation. Surely this is true when we are dealing with a program such as this initiated by the federal government.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It is not surprising to me that provincial governments are looking with a good deal of scepticism and a good deal of concern at shared cost programs, because it is pretty easy for the federal government to say to the provinces: We are prepared to pay half of the costs if you will come into this with us. Very often the provinces think it is a good idea, particularly when the federal government is going to help pay for the costs. However, if at some time in the future, one, two or five years later, the federal government decides suddenly and on its own that it is going to get out and let the provinces carry the burden, a burden which may well run into hundreds of millions of dollars, it is not surprising to me that some provincial governments might say: Under the circumstances and in the light

April 24, 1967
Occupational Training
of past experience we are not going to go ahead with this. At present this does not seem likely but it would not surprise me very much if in view of the way this problem has been handled the provinces said to the federal government: We are afraid to go into the medicare plan because although you might agree now to pay 50 per cent of the costs, three or five years from now you might say that health is a provincial matter and leave it to us to handle on our own. I am not saying the federal government has done this, and I for one would certainly have been sorry if they had done it. I am glad that nearly every province has indicated it is going into the medicare plan. However, as regards this decision on technical-vocational training made, as I said and I know I am right, without any consultation with the provinces, both with regard to the principle and to the details, it is not surprising that, to say the least, the provinces are very unhappy with the present situation. I urge the Minister of Manpower and Immigration-who is not here today, and I will not be too critical because I know that none of us expected this debate to begin tonight-to follow the example he set in the white paper on immigration. It is not too late. I do not think anyone will quarrel with the expansion of the program, although as I said earlier I think the division between education and manpower training is an artificial one which does not really exist.
Nevertheless, it is not too late for the federal government and for the department to sit down with the provinces, to go over the objections which they might have, to try to meet these objections, and to work out a program which will not only be accepted by the provinces, because they have no choice -after all the provinces are interested in getting as much financial assistance from the federal government as they can in this program as in every other program-but to work out a program which will meet the legitimate doubts, fears and objections of the provinces because, with all due respect to the officials in the federal department-and I know there are some very competent people there-they are not the ones who have had the experience in the field of educating young people or retraining older people for jobs. Who has had the most experience in this field? It is the provincial departments of education, the boards of education and the schoolboards in larger cities such as Toronto, Hamilton, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Calgary and Edmonton.
[Mr. Orlikow.l
It seems to me that the experience of these agencies and bodies, their know-how regarding what mistakes we should not and need not make, has been completely ignored, according to information which I have. Not only has it been ignored but apparently it has been rejected by the federal department.
I will say again in closing that it is not too late for the minister and for his department to take the time to discuss the details of the program and how it is to work with the provinces and with the people who are working in the field. Right here in Ottawa there are people who have had a great deal of experience in adult retraining. They have not been consulted. The same is true in Toronto and other places. I suggest to the minister, before we get much further with the bill, that he and his officials take the time to sit down with the interested agencies and get advice from them, so that the program can be improved.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on Bill No. C-278, although I have not yet had time to read it and our leader would have been far more able than I to comment on it generally. Still, it is obvious at first glance, that this bill will certainly give rise to several questions, will lead to discussions, not only while under study but even more so when it is implemented.
A while ago, I heard the previous speaker who, naturally enough, spoke as a socialist. He probably would have like the federal government to take over the whole field and manage it as it sees fit. But we, who are not of that opinion at all, and who are here first of all to protect the interests of the provinces in their fields of jurisdiction, ask whether the minister first consulted the provinces when he considered introducing this bill. I wonder whether this bill is not again the work of federal bureaucracy coming to the provinces and telling them: Here is a bill we have drafted; you may either accept it or reject it. If you accept it, you will derive some benefits; if you reject it, you will get nothing at all.
I believe that if the minister had been consistent before bringing in such a bill, he would have invited the representatives of the different provinces, during federal-provincial conferences, to give serious consideration to the legislation, in view of the fact that this is another one of those shared costs fields, in which provinces are as much interested as, if not more so, than the federal government. It seems to me that it would have been highly logical for the minister to consult the provincial representatives before starting out to draft such a bill.
Personally, we are wondering if Quebec will accept once again the conditions laid down by the federal government under this bill.
As usual, though, the federal government comes in through the back door. It reminds me somewhat of that man who under the pretext of bringing a box of matches to the woman of the house who needs them, puts the whole house on Are once inside.
I feel that if the federal government truly recognizes that education comes under provincial jurisdiction, it should leave it to the provinces. It should give back to them the means to administer those fields; it should 23033-9651
Occupational Training
first of all withdraw from their taxation field because it is another excuse for levying another tax. It should withdraw from provincial taxation fields and give back to the provinces in all fairness what belongs to them. Then, Mr. Speaker, it will be seen that the provinces are just as able as the federal government to give the required and appropriate education to their people.
Here, it is said that the provinces will be consulted in due course on such projects; but when the government for instance, is dealing with the employers on their relations with their employees, I wonder whether the provinces will have a word to say or whether the federal government will deal directly with the employers, with the large companies anxious to have their manpower trained in certain skills.
In this regard, if during consideration of this clause, we realize that the provincial governments will not be consulted when the question dealing with the employers arises, we shall certainly be opposed. We will not be in a position to accept such a clause and we will object to the federal government dealing directly with an employer, whatever his importance may be.
As far as assistance is concerned, it seems to me that, according to the bill, this will consist in paying for the training. But there all kinds of additional expenses, for instance, rental of premises, school construction, as mentioned further in the bill, purchase of equipment, etc.
I wonder whether, after all, the provinces will not be contributing the lion's share once again. And the federal government will say: Well, we have given you such and such a thing. But the provinces and their citizens will be paying three times the value of what they will have received. We find that the federal government is willing to grant or rather to guarantee the loans made to provinces to enable them to build facilities and schools, give those courses and buy equipment, but it will still be the provinces, since the federal government is no longer able to borrow money, which will borrow for a period of 20, 25 or 30 years and will once again be burdened with those debts from which, the federal government will perhaps have taken 50 per cent of its funds, while saying: We are the ones who have paid for those buildings.
A bill such as this, Mr. Speaker, always; seems to bring on new taxes. That is the reason why we are asking so many questions^

April 24, 1967
Occupational Training
We are well aware, looking at the history of the various governments which succeeded one another here, that when a government wants to help the people, it promises them two dollars but extorts five from them.
These are the points which we wished to call to the attention of the minister. We will keep our eyes open in order to see what advantages the Canadian people will reap from this. I am one hundred per cent in favour of training, but if the country does not benefit from this training, we shall have to think twice about it. I say that because precisely I received letters, four or five letters from young people and adults in my riding who after having attended refresher courses last winter or two years ago, have been unable to get a job. They cannot find a job, even with their competency card. It is very well to have 90 per cent of the population educated but it is better to have 100 per cent of the people employed.
Everyone knows that despite all our efforts in the field of education, our young people are deserting the province of Quebec which pays for their instruction, their education. In fact, one thousand, fifteen hundred and even two thousand technicians are leaving every year for our neighbour country to earn their living, after we have defrayed 100 per cent of the cost of their education and training.
In addition to this proposed training, which is good by the way, as long as we remain within the limits of delegated powers, my contention is that the government should also take into account those who are going to graduate, in order to provide them with a job on the day after they obtain their certificate.
Mr. Speaker, we will certainly have further comments to make, as we examine this bill clause by clause, but I simply want to warn the government that it should not act like in the past, in short this should not be another opportunity to intrude a little further in matters of provincial jurisdiction.

speechtext:
One becomes a bit pessimistic of these opening statements on second readings of bills, Mr. Speaker, that are presented with considerable flourish and skill, along with promises of a new world beginning with the passing of legislation in whatever area may be the subject matter of the bill. When one examines this bill, it becomes clear why the premier of British Columbia objected to the

dropping of the shared cost programs following the last federal-provincial fiscal conference. There is one thing about a shared cost program; it becomes a little difficult to sort out who pays for what. I suppose that in some ways it is more desirable for the federal government to announce that they are going directly into the field of adult education, because it does become more apparent how large or how small is their contribution in that particular area.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
We know that the premier of British Columbia is not alone in his concern about the changeover from shared cost programs to this type of program. For we are told that eight out of the ten provinces involved have already told the federal government that there will be serious difficulty with the bill that is before us this evening. Why should we be optimistic about the bill, Mr. Speaker, in view of the gaps that developed in the implementation of the Canada Assistance Plan? Why should we be optimistic about what is going to happen with adult education in view of some of the gaps that are developing in the implementation of the guaranteed annual income program in so far as it ties in, or rather fails to tie in, with the Canada Assistance Plan? For example, some of the funds for this program are being borrowed from the War Veterans Allowance Act, instead of being provided under the guaranteed annual income program.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the concern about this legislation that has been brought to my attention in a letter from the secretary-treasurer of the board of trustees for school district No. 22 at Vernon, British Columbia. In a letter addressed to Hon. L,. R. Peterson, the minister of education at Victoria, they express very great concern over the problems created at the local level by the passing of Bill No. C-278. They go on to say:
With the withdrawal of grants in aid for vocational and upgrading courses it is practically impossible to provide courses of this nature at a fee that the general public can afford to pay.
We would therefore urge the provincial government to continue the system of grants for vocational courses being offered through our adult education department as has been done in the past.
At the moment, Mr. Speaker, neither the minister in British Columbia nor the minister in any other province can answer this letter because the bill has not been passed. However, I am sure that after we do pass it provincial ministers will still have great
April 24, 1967

difficulty in answering any similar letter to this, as they await the implementation of the various clauses in this bill. Again I see very little cause for optimism, that the transition from the previous vocational training subsidies paid by the federal government to the payments provided under this legislation will be smooth.
I feel that the provisions in this legislation dealing with the classification and ages of adults show a serious lack of concern for, or knowledge of, the school rhythm as pupils move through from the system. It is common practice across this country to set the age of 15 as that at which compulsory education ends. The age may be raised to 16 in some provinces, though by no means in every province in Canada.
Anyone who has worked in a school, Mr. Speaker, knows that a great many who become eligible for this kind of program are just waiting for the day when they can leave school. This is not necessarily a criticism of the school system; it is in a way a fact of life. They wait for this day, and by the time they are 15, many of them have been waiting nine years until the day they could leave, at 15. It is not going to mean anything to these people when you tell them; "Perhaps you had better not leave yet, because if you leave now you will not be considered an adult by the federal government; you will have to wait three years. Therefore you had better stay in the school system for another three years".
Despite the hopes of the department of manpower in presenting this bill, I am aware that this sort of admonition to the teenager who has waited seven, eight or nine years to leave school will not be sufficient to retain him in the ordinary school system for a further three years, and he will leave regardless.
One of the previous speakers referred to the only road that opens up to early admission into the program. The teenagers of this country will need neither the previous speaker nor myself to tell them that they can quickly find a way out; that if they happen to have someone wholly or substantially dependant upon them for support they will then be able to qualify.
Although I think it is very much the role of the federal government to concern itself with adult education and with vocational training, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is the role of the federal government openly to encourage early marriage, as this bill does. I think all of the family planners, juvenile courts and
Occupational Training
school counsellors across this country are united in their efforts to postpone early marriage for any of these people. Yet we have in this bill a policy which these people will be very quick to see enables them to qualify for the program two years and three months sooner than they would otherwise have qualified for retraining assistance.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, these teenagers would not even need to move away from home. We already know that many of these early marriages are supported in part by the parents of the young people involved. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there is built into the bill the incentive to marry early in this country.
We might also ask why the legislation does not spell out a little more clearly that private training courses will be used fully as well as the public school system. This is an area of education which private enterprise began to develop very early in Canada, and developed to a very great extent. There are many occupational groups which are served entirely, or virtually entirely, by private training schools. I think of hairdressing as one example, and there is of course the business field. There is tremendous involvement on the part of private enterprise there.
The Association of Canadian Commercial Colleges is not satisfied with the provisions of this bill as they have been announced. They would like some emendation so as to include the idea that it is highly desirable to employ the resources of the private sector of the economy of Canada in all such efforts to further the policy of this bill. In spite of the reassurances given by the parliamentary secretary this evening, I think it would be of interest to this group and to the members of this house to have these reassurances spelt out a little more clearly.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Again, Mr. Speaker, why should we be optimistic about this government's concern for private enterprise in view of the problems which will be created with the proposed future implementation of the medicare scheme? Why should we be optimistic when we know that this government's attitude to private enterprise has been that private enterprise is either an unmitigated evil, or at best a necessary evil? Why should these schools find any reassurance in the bill presently before us?
Another area of legislation concerns me very much. It is that part to be found in clause 13 of the bill which reads:
Where a person has received a training allowance to which he is not entitled or a training

April 24, 1967
Occupational Training
allowance in an amount in excess of the training allowance to which he is entitled, the amount thereof or the excess amount, as the case may be, may be recovered at any time as a debt due to Her Majesty or may be retained, in whole or in part, out of any subsequent amount payable to that person as a training allowance.
Why should we be optimistic about what will happen once this bill is implemented, considering what happened under the old age security legislation and the War Veterans Allowance Act. This government has persistently gone after people who through no fault of their own have received overpayments. What criteria will be used to recover repayments made under retraining courses? Will a person be charged with having accepted an overpayment if, through no fault of his own, he is forced to drop out?
Worse than that, will the government inveigle people to come back and finish their courses, that the overpayment paid to them may in some mysterious way be recovered? Will the strange system of bookkeeping be used by which the government imagines that by providing courses and withholding part of its allowances it will in some strange way recover overpayments?
It would be better if in the future we could introduce in this country a system of primary education that, beginning with kindergarten levels, will make sure that the education given to people is effective education. We ought to find ways and means to encourage the right people to take up teaching; we ought to have great numbers of the right sorts of teachers, that our young people beginning .school may not be frustrated, may not be short changed, but may receive a sound foundation in education. By doing that we should reduce the need for the type of retraining programs that affect people later in life.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF COSTS, AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate to discuss the important measure before us. As my colleague, the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Regimbal) said a little earlier in the debate, the government might be criticized on the ground that seven weeks have passed since Bill C-278 was introduced. This is one of the most important measures to have come before this house for a good many years because it deals with the lives of so many of our citizens.
Before proceeding with my remarks I wish to commend the former minister of labour, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), for the very fine and constructive measure he

introduced when he was minister, the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act. In doing my homework for this speech I read the minister's speeches on this subject, and I thought they were excellent.
It is easy to understand why this measure is before us. The effects of technological change are being felt more and more every year. Recently, when somebody commented on the year that has just passed, 1966, he said that it would be known in years to come as the year of the strikes. We had many crippling strikes in this country last year. Some of those were for higher wages, some were caused by union rivalry but it seems to me that in no small measure many strikes were caused by something not so evident, that is, unrest and the fear of working men who see that their skills are no longer in demand. It is tragic to see men who for many years have worked well with their hands being told one day that they are not wanted. Many of those men have families.
When I was home during this past week end I saw a delegation of railwaymen who were deeply concerned because two trains were being taken off the Canadian National Railway. It was the old story: More can be done with the big diesels than ever could be done in the days of steam. One man told me that he had worked on the railway for 26 years, had six children, and had been laid off. He would not be able to find steady work. This sort of thing causes a feeling of unrest among our workingmen, and that in turn causes some strikes.
Let me talk of automation. I was born on a farm, and as a young man I can well remember how lumbering was carried on. Of course the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) one of the most proficient lumbermen in eastern Canada is more competent to speak on lumbering than I am. In my boyhood it took two men with a cross-cut saw to cut down a tree. A few years later came the chain saw enabling one man to do three or four or five times the work that a man with the cross-cut saw had done. Tractors replaced horses; and so it went. Men who were in demand on the railroad and lumbering industries are being told that there are no more jobs for them.
We in the House of Commons are on the mailing list for every publication, probably, in the country. In a recent issue of the Ontario Logger magazine, an article said that one man operating a logging machine which had taken ten years to develop and which cost a third of a million of dollars could do as
April 24, 1967

much work as scores of men had done previously.
All that the operator, who is enclosed in an air conditioned cab-and that is a far cry from the old conditions-has to do is to select the trees. The machine will remove the bark, limb the tree, cut it into eight foot lengths and stack them along the road. One man with one of these machines can do in one hour what it would have taken more than 20 hours to do with a chain saw. There we have an example of what has happened in a basic industry.
I am interested in this measure because I am a teacher in the field of technical and vocational training, and this bill deals with that subject. A few years ago I took part in an interesting experiment in the retraining of workers. In my constituency there is a cotton milling town named Marysville. Some 12 or 15 years ago, due I believe to financial difficulties encountered by the parent company, the mill was closed and many workers were thrown out of employment. This mill had been in operation for almost 100 years and generations had worked in it. When their employment ceased they had no skills except those of cotton workers.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The minister of labour at that time was Hon. Milton Gregg, V.C. who represented my constituency. Later he became a political opponent, although we have always remained the closest of friends. He arranged with private industry and the department of education of the province of New Brunswick to retrain these people who had lost their jobs in the mill. I personally took some 30 or 40-I forget the exact number-and retrained them in office skills. The scheme worked very well. Unfortunately, a few of them did not have the necessary basic education, and this was the only reason they did not succeed. The rest worked hard at their courses and the great majority of them are still working, using the skills in which they were trained at that time.
It is impressed upon us every time the subject of education arises that education is a provincial matter under the terms of the British North America Act. The province from which the minister comes, the province of Quebec, which is also the province of my birth, is more conscious of this particular right than any of the others, and guards it more jealously. But I have reached the conclusion with the passing of the years that when we rewrite our constitution, as eventually we shall have to do, this is a situation which we
Occupational Training
shall have to change to some extent. In 1867 when this nation was formed people travelled very little. They grew up, married and died, not more than a few miles from the village in which they had been born. Now we travel back and forth across this continent in a few hours. A few years ago I taught a student, a soldier's daughter, who in the course of 12 years had gone to 15 different schools. It is surprising that this child had done so well in her studies. If we are to have ten systems of education it will be necessary to find some way of co-ordinating education in this country of ours.
I wish now to make a plea on behalf of a very special group of educators who are interested in this measure. The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke drew attention to the fact that there is in this country a very special group of private educators, the private business school people. Several hundred of them are meeting here in May and bringing distinguished educators from Britain and from the United States to their convention. I want to put the following facts on record for the benefit of the minister, his parliamentary secretary and those who are doing the work of the department.
The private business colleges of this country can do, and have been doing for more than a hundred years, a completely efficient job in the field of adult training and retraining. Many members of this House of Commons in the course of achieving an education have gone to private business schools to learn the business skills. Business colleges are established throughout this country and are grouped in an association known as the Association of Canadian Commercial Colleges. They are very much aware of the problems involved in adult education and are able to adjust quickly to solving them. Many of them are already participating in program five training, that is, the training of the unemployed. and equipment available, and they also have the staff capable of undertaking these services.

There is nothing wrong about the government purchasing the services of private enterprise in connection with any endeavour upon which it has embarked. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the time allotted to us under the rules at this point is very limited I shall deal with this question as quickly as possible. On April 3 I addressed the following question to the Minister of
April 24, 1967

Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet), as recorded at page 14421 of Hansard:
Is the hon. gentleman aware of the charges and accusations that have been made that legitimate, pensionable veterans have been refused bed space in the Camp Hill Hospital while merchant seamen from Canada and other countries are occupying beds? Will he investigate this matter?
The minister replied:
I have certainly not heard of this. I will look into it but I very much doubt the accuracy of that report.
I followed this up with a question to the acting minister on April 5, which he took as notice. On April 10 I again brought it to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs and he very kindly stated that he was having an investigation carried out regarding a particular case. At that point I brought to his attention the fact that the hospital director, Dr. C. J. MacDonald, according to a report in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of Wednesday, April 5, even before the minister had a chance to report to the house, had given this statement to the press:
"Veterans have always had priority of admission *-and always will have," he said. "In fact, we have never found it necessary to refuse admission to anybody. While we have been short of beds, we have never been without them."
So apparently all these complaints I have received mean only one thing, that everybody is out of step but Charlie. Again the minister very kindly on April 19 gave a somewhat similar reply, and at that time I indicated I would like to deal with the question at the adjournment of the house, under the rules, which I am now doing.
This problem was first brought to my attention by a veteran in the town of Sydney Mines, and I would like to put his letter on record. I might say that he is a 100 per cent pensioner. His letter reads:
Having been a pensioner for a number of years, and going back and forth to Camp Hill up until 1960, and receiving good treatment, on March 7th of this year I had need to go to Camp Hill hospital for treatment. But on word from the D.V.A. doctor in Sydney, Dr. Ross, that there were no beds for me in Camp Hill, I finally told him I had to go. He then told me to go and when I reached there, the same story would be related to me of no beds.
After a lot of discussion and dickering, I finally received a bed.
When I was able to move about, I found out that if you are not a veteran you will receive a bed more promptly than a veteran.
In one room there were three Russians, Turks, Spaniards, and to top it all, Chinese doctors that were almost impossible to understand. I don't think this is one bit fair to a veteran. The country 23033-966
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
doesn't owe us everything but at least we should be provided with a place to die in peace.
We were, at one time, proud of our hospital until we were sold down the river by someone.
Will you please let me know if we have any right to a bed in what used to be our hospital, or not, and what priority we have.
Enos Ashe,
136 Fraser Avenue, Sydney Mines, N.S.
Incidentally that gentleman is a member of the town council of Sydney Mines and is quite prepared to appear before the minister, or any inquiry at any place, at any time, to support his statements.
Following this I received a letter from Wilbert Hupman of R. R. 1, Port Mouton, Queens County, Nova Scotia. It is as follows:
Dear Sir, I am writing you re your statement in the Commons concerning veterans in Camp Hill. This is 100 per cent true in some cases as it happened to me also. I do not believe in unnecessarily complaining, but this is carrying things very recklessly and if	it	keeps	up	where can aveteran turn for help.	I	was more	than pleasedthat someone brought	this to	the	attention ofthose responsible and	I	have	also	written the
veterans minister. In closing I wish to thank you for bringing this to light.
Then I should like to quote this portion of a letter from a person named Lawrence Walker of Summerville, Hants County, Nova Scotia:
I am a veteran of two wars. I thought Camp Hill was established for us, but I find it half full of fishermen.
Further on in the letter he says:
What to my mind is needed is a board of inquiry where we can testify to what is going on.
I also note this letter to the editor, from one Bernard O'Neil of Digby:
Sir: Having just arrived home from Camp Hill Hospital I should like to make some comments about the hospital as I observed it while I was there for about a week.
First of all, I feel that veterans who served their country in time of war are not getting a fair shake at Camp Hill.
While it may be true that veterans are not refused, they certainly get deferred, sometimes for a month.
In my own case an attempt was made to defer me, but my local doctor pressed the matter and I was admitted.
When I arrived in Camp Hill I found that there were a number of beds empty. Also I discovered that there were a number of compensation cases who were not veterans, who were patients in the hospital.
I was also told that beds were being occupied by marine insurance cases, also non-veterans.
As far as treatment and care are concerned, I feel that there is insufficient staff, particularly medical staff, at Camp Hill. The doctors are definitely overworked and sometimes cannot get

April 24, 1967
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion to examine or treat the patient until he has been in hospital tor several days.
In my own case, I was at Camp Hill for four days before I was examined. My bed went unmade for two days even though I asked to have it made.
Although I am a D-Day veteran and served overseas until V-E Day and am also a pensioner, I was advised I would have to pay a fee for doctors' services while at Camp Hill. I understand this fee is based on patient earnings and is a custom which has only recently been instituted.
I do want to say in defence of Camp Hill that the food was very good while I was there and the staff was most friendly and kind, even though badly overworked.
Here again everybody is out of step but Charlie.
I have here a clipping from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of April 8, 1967. The heading is "DVA Is Criticized at Legion Zone Meeting" and it is as follows:
The Department of Veterans Affairs was criticized at a meeting of Zone 12, Canadian Legion, in Clark's Harbour, presided over by zone commander John Freeman, of Sable River.

Then further on:
Several veterans told of being released from Camp Hill Hospital without, what they claimed to be, proper justice.
In conclusion Mr. Brown urged branches to send delegates to the Sydney Convention.
Mr. Speaker, all I ask the minister, who has been very courteous, is whether he would refer this matter to the standing committee on veterans affairs, and then if everything is in order, as suggested by the minister and the doctor in charge of the hospital, no one has anything to worry about. I would suggest that this would be the way to clear up the matter once and for all.

speakeroldname: Hon. Roger Teillel (Minister of Veierans Affairs):
maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-CAMP HILL, N.S.- REPORT OF LACK OF HOSPITAL ACCOMMODATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept unreservedly the attitude of the hon. member; that is, he is interested in the welfare of our veterans of Canada and the presentation he is making this evening is simply in an effort to help us provide the kind of service which we all believe the veterans of Canada should have. My answer to him will be in the spirit of that idea.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I fully appreciate that our people are overworked and understaffed, and that we have difficulty in finding the professional staff to

man our hospitals. The hon. member has underlined the quality and the spirit of our hospitals. While these people are overworked they do go out of their way to serve the veterans of Canada.
Let me place a few facts on the record. There is always a bed available for the admission of a veteran for treatment of a pensionable disability, and such veterans have first priority if prompt admission is medically indicated. After the treatment of pensionable disabilities, the next priority is in respect of persons whose treatment is the responsibility of other departments of the federal government. We have a responsibility in this regard. The next priority is the treatment of various categories of veterans for non-pensionable disabilities, and eligibility usually involves their type of service and financial circumstances.
It is the responsibility of the department and doctors to determine whether treatment in a departmental hospital is required, whether it is for a pensionable or non-pensionable disability, and whether the admission is urgent or elective.
For part of last winter Camp Hill hospital was operated at almost full capacity. Indeed additional beds had to be set up to accommodate all admissions. However, at no time was admission for treatment of a pensionable disability, which was required immediately, delayed or denied. This can also be said in respect of treatment for non-pensionable disabilities.
For a short period during this winter, admissions which were not urgent were postponed briefly to a more appropriate time, in the interests of best treatment. The complaints received make it appear that these decisions on the basis of the opinion of departmental medical officers were sometimes in conflict with the wishes of the veterans, who desired immediate admission, even though they were not immediately medically necessary.
I conclude by thanking my hon. friend for giving me this opportunity to put these facts on the record in order to clear up any misunderstanding which may have occurred.

WATER RESOURCES-PARTICIPATION BY CANADA IN "WATER FOR PEACE" CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I appreciate the presence of the minister here this evening. I congratulate him for the work he has done in
April 24, 19G7

his department in connection with this very important question of a national water policy, and I congratulate him for his part in organizing the conference held a few months ago on pollution in our environment. The speeches he has made throughout the country indicate his concern about this whole question, and I congratulate him for his work in reorganizing certain administrative features to deal with this whole problem more efficiently and effectively in years ahead.
Let me say that the minister and I have a sort of mutual disability. We both suffer from water on the brain. This very important question of water pollution is one of concern to many Canadians at this time. Water is priceless, and it is becoming of more importance every day.
One can exaggerate the value of many things, but not the value of water. Not one plant, animal, or even a beautiful woman can exist without it. We cannot maintain or improve our living standards without an ample supply of pure water. Without any doubt our health and our recreational facilities for generations to come will depend on action by the federal, provincial and municipal governments in the very near future.
This matter was again brought to my attention quite recently by an article which appeared in the April 22 issue of the Financial Post written by Mr. Clive Baxter, and entitled "Water, water everywhere

and Ottawa knows why". It reads as follows:
Canada will be represented in force at the big Water for Peace Conference in Washington May 23-31-but the lack of enthusiasm could show through.
It is no secret the Canadian government was miffed when President Johnson announced the 60-nation conference two years ago-without bothering to consult the other governments. It forced everyone's hand and Ottawa was annoyed.
Until Ottawa and the provinces can agree on a long-term water-export policy, federal officials have been sidestepping suggestions from any source that a U.S.-Canada water conference might be useful. When the Water for Peace meeting was scheduled, there suddenly appeared the dangerous prospect of "talks within talks" that could put the Canadian delegation in the position of having to take a stand on transborder water sales.
When it was learned the conference organizers were planning a North American regional session, the danger suddenly appeared acute. Ottawa immediately objected and managed to get that part of the agenda changed.
It now appears likely that embarrassing confrontations can be avoided. The agenda is suitably broad to make bilateral water discussions inappropriate if not impossible.
Canada's delegation will comprise federal and provincial government representatives. Energy, Mines and Resources Minister Jean-Luc Pepin told
15279
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion FP they will go to Washington with an agreed Canadian position on the need to co-operate on the whole question of water use, hoping to set a good example to other federal states in battling pollution and water waste.
Then the article goes on to deal with other aspects of this conference. I trust that when our delegation goes to Washington it will be united in agreement, because without a doubt they will find the United States delegation united and determined in their actions with respect to the years ahead.
I just want to quote from a very interesting book which was recently published, entitled "Water, The Vital Essence". It indicates how important it is at the present time that our delegation goes in agreement and stands united. I will quote this from page 209 of the book.
An official in the United States, who shall otherwise be unidentified, was once heard to suggest that the ultimate solution to the water supply problems of the northeastern United States would be to divert large amounts from lakes in the Province of Ontario-and that if Canada should object, then the United States would simply have to take it over.
I have the transcript of that address and the name of the person who stated that. It goes on to read:
Canadians are perfectly aware of the interest of the United States in their water. In spite of strong political opposition, Prime Minister Pearson has been willing to discuss the matter. "The United States," he said in a televised address, "is finding that water is one of its most valuable, and becoming one of its scarcest, resources, and we have- well, we have lots of water." "Exporting water", he said, "can be as important as exporting wheat or oil. This can be one of the most important developments in our history." An official inventory is being taken in Canada, which has one-sixth of the world's fresh water supply, to see how much could be spared from its two great northflowing river systems, the Mackenzie and Nelson, or from the province of Ontario, where one acre out of every ten is under water.
I am quite sure that since the present minister has taken office the Prime Minister would not make a statement similar to the one he made on television during that election. However, it is because of this concern that I asked the minister the following question on April 21:
I wish to address a question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
At that time the minister was absent on official business.
Can the minister inform the house the number of federal and provincial government representatives who will be attending the Water for Peace Conference in Washington from May 23 to May 31 this year, and can the minister inform the house whether these delegates will have an agreed
1S280	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Canadian position on water policy, water pollution and water waste?
[DOT] (10:20 p.ra.)
It was at that point, Mr. Speaker, that you shot me down and forced me to stay late this evening in order to get an answer to my question. Let me say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that Canada expects every member of the Canadian delegation to this conference to do his duty on this occasion.

The second part of the question has to do with the policy we are going to uphold during that meeting. May I underline that the "Water for Peace" conference is not an intergovernmental negotiating or policy making meeting. As a matter of fact, Canada would not have accepted an invitation to that kind of meeting. This will be a rather informal gathering at ministerial and technical levels for the purpose of exchanging information and ideas, and of fostering co-operation between different countries and different parts of the world. Consequently, there is no

DEBATES	April 24, 1967
need for absolute unanimity or uniformity of views as between the members of the Canadian delegation.
There will be, however, a "country position paper". It will be a review of the Canadian situation with regard to water. This Canadian paper has been prepared by a national committee made up of representatives of the federal and provincial governments. To speak very frankly, the paper will be a descriptive paper of what exists in Canada and is not a policy making paper. It is more descriptive than anything else.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, on orders of the day, I put a question to the hon. Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauv6) because last weekend an extremely important event took place on the lower St. Lawrence.
A meeting was held at Cabano of representatives from three counties comprising the nine ridings which make up the pilot area of the lower St. Lawrence, Gaspe peninsula and Magdelene Islands. It was decided, by a majority vote, that a council would be organized but that this council would remain independent from the rest of the area in order to pursue the specific objectives of the three counties, namely Kamouraska, Riviere-du-Loup and Temiscouata.
The reason why I raised this question is that it fits into the framework of the general plan of the lower St. Lawrence and Gasp6 Peninsula Development Board.
As we know, the federal government, through the ARDA act, administered by the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development contributed 50 per cent of the cost of those studies. The cost of such studies was considerable at $4 million and the 50 per cent federal contribution, under ARDA, will amount to something like $2 million.
Therefore, it is very much in our interest that this project as put forward by the Eastern Quebec Development Board should
April 24, 1967	COMMONS
be implemented. But before discussing that particular problem of bringing the structures of the plan into being, I would like to recall the six objectives mentioned in the development plan. I quote:
1.	Modernize traditional basic fields (fanning, fishing and partly forestry) in which is found the concern for redevelopment, the utilization of resources contained in the second alternative;
That is the alternative where all the resources of the territory would be fully used.
2.	Create new dynamic activities (tourism, industry and mining) which imply that considerable efforts will be made in those fields to keep the territory's population at a minimum of 325,000 people where it is economically realistic to supply them with the urban services they want;
3.	Increase the value of manpower seeking to establish the geographical and vocational mobility required by the contemplated development and use of resources, the promotion of proposed new undertakings and the accepted rate of emigration.
4.	Establish a planning and participating institutional framework likely to provide an institutional basis for the planned regional development in cooperation with the population;
5.	Build up a regional awareness which will result in a popular sharing in the objectives and the method of proposed development and, finally;
6.	Rationalize the regional area to provide at a practical cost the regional population with the urban services they hope for and which will create the basic conditions essential to the development of certain sectors, particularly tourism and industry.
The fourth objective, the establishment of a local body to implement the plan is precisely the subject of discussions between the various sectors of the region.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
I wish to point out that the decision made by the Grand-Portage area with regard to the three counties of Kamouraska, Riviere-du-Loup and Temiscouata, may not meet the legitimate wishes of the people of the area, but that such a stand should perhaps not be considered as jeopardizing the implementation of the program in the whole territory. That is the point I want the minister to answer.
Mr. Speaker, this very costly plan has also given rise within the population to great aspirations towards improved economic conditions, and the people should not be deprived of advantages they normally expect because of the partial implementation of that program.
It may also be necessary to somewhat restrict the scope of the original plan, so that we, from other sections of the area, from Matapedia-Matane, may be able to contribute to the achievement of those aims. I know
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion that the federal government has not only helped to finance these studies but already begun talks with the authorities of the province of Quebec concerning the implementation of this program.
